flawed_step: Step 3: The attempted proof assumes that the arc between the endpoints of the Hamiltonian path is directed v4→v1; the tournament definition does not determine this orientation.
counterexample: Take vertices {1,2,3,4} and orient every edge i→j exactly when i<j. This is a tournament, but every directed path has strictly increasing labels, so it has no directed cycle and hence no Hamiltonian cycle.
assessment_summary:
1. Every finite tournament has a directed Hamiltonian path; thus write one as v1→v2→v3→v4. JUSTIFIED: Inductively insert each new vertex x into an existing directed path: prepend x if x points to the first vertex, append it if the last vertex points to x, and otherwise insert it at a transition vi→x→v(i+1).
2. Exactly one of v4→v1 and v1→v4 is an arc of T. JUSTIFIED: This follows directly from the definition of a tournament.
3. Assert that v4→v1. NOT JUSTIFIED: Step 2 permits the opposite orientation v1→v4, and no preceding fact rules it out.
4. Conclude that v1→v2→v3→v4→v1 is a Hamiltonian cycle. NOT JUSTIFIED AS A PROOF OF THE CLAIM: The conclusion would follow conditionally from Step 3, but Step 3 was not established.
5. Consider instead the tournament on {1,2,3,4} having i→j precisely when i<j. JUSTIFIED: Every pair of distinct labels has exactly one such oriented arc, so this is a tournament on exactly four vertices.
6. Every directed path in this tournament has strictly increasing vertex labels. JUSTIFIED: By its construction, each arc goes from the smaller label to the larger label.
7. This tournament contains no directed cycle. JUSTIFIED: Traversing a directed cycle would require labels to increase strictly at every step and nevertheless return to the starting label, which is impossible.
8. Therefore this tournament has no Hamiltonian cycle, and the stated universal claim is false. JUSTIFIED: A Hamiltonian cycle is a directed cycle, while Step 7 shows that this tournament has none.
